opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the starting point was this idea Yann had been articulating: instead of predicting pixels, you predict in representation space. Conceptually that's clean, but when you actually sit down to build it for images, you have to make a lot of concrete decisions, and those decisions end up mattering a lot.

The first question was what the "x" and the "y" should be. In a lot of self-supervised work at the time, especially the joint-embedding methods, you'd take two augmented views of the same image and ask the network to make their embeddings agree. That works well, but it leans heavily on hand-crafted augmentations like color jitter, cropping, and blurring, and those encode a lot of human priors about what should be invariant. We wanted to see if we could get away from that. So instead of augmentations, we used masking within a single image. You take one context block from the image, and from that you try to predict the representations of several target blocks elsewhere in the same image.

The second piece was making sure the prediction happens in latent space and not pixel space. We have a context encoder, a Vision Transformer, that processes only the visible context patches. Then a target encoder, which is an exponential moving average of the context encoder, processes the full image, and we pull out the representations corresponding to the target blocks. A separate predictor network takes the context representation plus positional information about where the targets are, and it has to predict those target representations. Because the targets are themselves learned features, the model isn't forced to model every little texture detail or bit of noise. It can focus on the more semantic, predictable structure.

Then a lot of the work was in the masking strategy, which was honestly one of the more surprising parts. If your target blocks are too small, the task becomes kind of low-level, almost like local interpolation. If your context is too small or too scattered, there isn't enough information to predict anything meaningful. What worked was using fairly large target blocks, so the model has to predict semantic content, and a reasonably large, spatially contiguous context block, with the target regions removed from it so there's no trivial overlap. That multi-block setup was really what got the representations to become semantic.

And of course there's the collapse question, which comes up with any joint-embedding approach. If both sides are learned, what stops everything from mapping to a constant? Here the asymmetry does a lot of the work: the predictor, the stop-gradient on the target side, and the EMA target encoder. Empirically that was enough to keep things stable.

What was exciting in the end was that you get strong off-the-shelf semantic representations, good on linear probing and on lower-level tasks too, without any hand-crafted augmentations, and quite efficiently in terms of compute, since you're not reconstructing pixels or processing multiple augmented views. That felt like a real validation that predicting in abstract representation space isn't just a nice philosophical idea but something that works in practice.

r001.rationale: The response says the context is one block from an image and the model predicts representations of target blocks elsewhere in that same image, identifying the differently masked portions as X and Y.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure, so the starting point was really Yann's position paper on autonomous machine intelligence, where JEPA is laid out as this very general idea: you have an encoder, you take some input x and some related input y, you embed both of them, and you train a predictor to predict the embedding of y from the embedding of x. The key thing is that the prediction happens in representation space, not in pixel space. You're not trying to reconstruct every detail of y, you're trying to predict an abstract representation of it, and ideally the encoder gets to discard the stuff that's unpredictable or just not semantically interesting.

That's a nice framework on paper, but it leaves a lot open. What are x and y concretely? What's the architecture? And the big one: how do you keep the whole thing from collapsing, because the trivial solution where the encoder outputs a constant makes the prediction task perfectly easy.

So when we built I-JEPA, the first decision was what x and y should be for images. We'd been doing a lot of work with masked image modeling at the time, so the natural instantiation was: take an image, split it into patches, define a context block, and then a few target blocks elsewhere in the image. The context encoder sees only the context block, and the predictor has to produce the representations of the target blocks, conditioned on where those targets are via positional tokens. The targets themselves come from a separate target encoder that sees the full image.

And the thing we found really matters is the masking strategy. If you make the targets too small or too scattered, the model can solve the task with low-level cues, like interpolating texture. So we used fairly large target blocks, sampled at reasonable scale, and a context block that's informative but spatially distinct from the targets. That forces the predictor to actually reason about what should be there semantically: this is a dog, so the occluded region probably contains a leg or an ear, at a representation level, without having to commit to the exact pixels.

The collapse question we handled with an asymmetric design. The target encoder is an exponential moving average of the context encoder, and gradients don't flow through it. That's borrowed from the self-supervised literature, from things like BYOL and our own work on MSN, and it turns out to be sufficient in practice. You don't need contrastive negatives, you don't need handcrafted augmentations like color jitter or random crops. That was important to us, because a lot of the invariance-based methods bake in priors about what shouldn't matter in an image, and we wanted something that learns more directly from the structure of the data.

And then the last piece, which is a bit mundane but mattered a lot, was making the predictor narrow relative to the encoder. You want the encoder to carry the representational capacity and the predictor to be a lightweight thing that just models the relationship between context and target. If the predictor is too big it starts doing the encoder's job.

So in a sense the approach was less about inventing new machinery and more about making a sequence of choices that are faithful to the original idea: predict in representation space, over meaningful chunks of the input, with as little handcrafted invariance as possible, and see whether the representations that come out are useful. And it turned out they were quite competitive on things like linear probing and low-shot ImageNet, and it trained a lot more efficiently than pixel-reconstruction methods, which was a nice confirmation that predicting in latent space is actually doing something.

r001.rationale: It describes a context block and separate target blocks elsewhere in the same image, with the predictor predicting the targets from the context.

astra-6.text:
The key question was: what should the model predict? If you predict pixels, you’re asking it to capture every little detail in an image, including things that may not matter for understanding what’s in the scene. With JEPA, we instead predict a representation of the missing content.

So we take an image, give one encoder a visible context region, and ask a predictor to predict the representations of other regions in that image. The targets come from a second encoder that sees the target content. The prediction happens entirely in representation space.

Of course, that creates a challenge: if both sides are learning, they could just output the same constant vector and make the prediction task trivial. So the way we update the target encoder, and how we construct the prediction task, are important. We use a slowly moving average of the context encoder to produce the targets, rather than training that encoder directly through the prediction loss.

And the masking strategy really matters. We want the target regions to be large enough that predicting them requires some understanding of the scene, while giving the model enough context to make that prediction meaningful. That’s how we turn the abstract idea into a concrete learning problem for images.

r001.rationale: It describes a visible context region and other target regions from the same image, with the target encoder seeing the target content and a masking strategy shaping the regions.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea was to take an image, hide part of it, and ask the model to predict a representation of the missing part from the context that’s visible. The important distinction is that we’re not trying to reconstruct the missing pixels. We’re predicting in a learned representation space, where the model can focus on more meaningful properties of the image.

So we have a context encoder that processes the visible patches, a target encoder that produces representations of the regions we want to predict, and a predictor that maps from the context to those target representations. The target encoder is updated as a moving average of the context encoder, which gives us a slowly evolving prediction target.

A key design choice was the masking strategy. We wanted the prediction task to require an understanding of the image, rather than just filling in a small gap using nearby texture. So we predict relatively large regions from a distributed context. That’s how we turned the abstract idea into a concrete learning objective for images.

r001.rationale: It describes visible patches as context and the masked, missing regions as prediction targets from the same image, matching the criterion’s X/Y relationship.
